name: Rear Naked Choke from Invisible Collar
summary: The Rear Naked Choke from Invisible Collar is a gi-based bait-and-switch: when the opponent commits both hands to stripping the concealed collar grip, the attacker releases it and threads the choking arm under the undefended chin to finish.
description: Master the Rear Naked Choke from Invisible Collar. Learn collar-to-RNC bait-and-switch transitions, finishing mechanics, and complete defensive guide.
overview:
Within high-level gi back-attack systems, this transition weaponizes the inherent deception of the invisible collar to manufacture a clean path to the neck. While the opponent commits defensive resources to removing the concealed collar grip, the attacker releases the collar and immediately threads the choking arm beneath the chin during the window when both of the defender's hands are occupied with the now-abandoned grip. This timing-dependent transition converts a gi-based positional threat into a universal finishing hold that bypasses conventional neck defense.

What distinguishes this technique from a standard Rear Naked Choke is the forced defensive reaction that precedes it. The invisible collar grip demands two-handed removal from the defender, creating a predictable moment where the neck is unprotected. Advanced practitioners use incremental collar deepening to escalate the perceived threat, drawing increasingly committed defensive responses that widen the transition window. The deeper the opponent believes the collar threat to be, the more aggressively they commit their hands to removal, and the more exposed they become to the RNC switch.

This submission functions as a critical component of back attack systems where the collar and RNC form a binary dilemma. Defending one attack directly enables the other, forcing the opponent into a lose-lose decision cycle. Competition-level practitioners chain this transition repeatedly, alternating between collar deepening and RNC attempts until the opponent's defensive timing deteriorates and the finish presents itself.

injury_risks.injury: Loss of consciousness from bilateral carotid compression
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate to 30 seconds with proper release

injury_risks.injury: Trachea damage from improper forearm placement across windpipe
Cervical spine strain from neck cranking during application
Carotid artery dissection from excessive or sudden force
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate medical attention required, potential stroke risk

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum in training. Never snap or jerk the choke. Partner should have full awareness of pressure building before compression becomes dangerous.
tap_signals: Verbal tap (say 'tap' or make any verbal sound indicating submission)
Physical hand tap on opponent's body, arm, or mat
Physical foot tap on mat when hands are trapped
Going limp or loss of consciousness requires immediate release
Any distress signal, unusual sound, or gurgling
release_protocol: Immediately release choking arm pressure upon any tap signal
Remove hooks and all lower body control
Gently guide partner to side-lying recovery position
Monitor consciousness and breathing for minimum 30 seconds
If partner lost consciousness, keep them lying down until fully alert and oriented
Never allow an unconscious partner to stand or sit up immediately
training_restrictions: Never apply competition speed or intensity during drilling
Never place forearm directly across the trachea or windpipe
Always ensure partner has clear tap access with at least one hand
Stop immediately if partner makes any distress sound or goes silent
Never hold a choke past the tap for any reason
Beginners must practice with extremely slow progressive pressure only

variations_and_setups.description: The standard collar-to-RNC switch where you release the collar grip and immediately thread the choking arm beneath the chin in one fluid motion. Relies on timing the release for maximum opponent hand commitment on the collar.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent has committed both hands to removing your collar grip and their chin is slightly elevated from the effort of stripping

variations_and_setups.description: Use the collar grip to pull the opponent's head and chin upward before releasing, creating additional space beneath the chin for the choking arm to enter. The upward collar pressure lifts the chin momentarily, widening the threading window.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent maintains a strong chin tuck that makes direct threading difficult, using the collar leverage to break their chin defense before switching

variations_and_setups.description: Establish a body triangle before initiating the collar-to-RNC switch to eliminate the opponent's ability to hip escape during the critical transition moment. The body triangle locks their lower body in place, allowing full focus on the upper body grip change.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against opponents who use explosive hip movement to create escape opportunities during grip transitions, the body triangle removes their primary escape mechanism

attacker.name: from Invisible Collar Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack with the Rear Naked Choke from Invisible Collar. Master collar-to-RNC switch timing, grip transition mechanics, and finishing details.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the Rear Naked Choke from Invisible Collar requires mastering the timing of the collar-to-RNC switch. The critical skill is reading when your opponent's hands are maximally committed to collar defense, then executing a seamless release-and-thread that bypasses their chin before they can redirect their hands to neck protection. This technique rewards patience during the collar phase and explosive precision during the transition window. Your supporting arm must maintain seatbelt structure throughout to prevent escape during the critical moment when your choking arm is in transit between collar and neck. The entire sequence depends on making the collar threat genuine enough to demand two-handed defense, then capitalizing on the opening that defense creates.
key_principles: Make the collar threat genuinely dangerous before attempting the RNC switch to force committed two-handed defense
Time the transition for the exact moment both opponent hands are engaged on your collar wrist and forearm
Maintain seatbelt control with the non-collar arm throughout the entire transition to preserve back control
Execute the release-and-thread as one continuous fluid motion rather than two separate actions
Keep hooks active and controlling during the upper body transition to prevent hip escape
Apply finishing pressure progressively through bilateral carotid compression, never across the trachea
Chain between collar deepening and RNC attempts to create an unsolvable dilemma cycle
setup_requirements: Established back control with at least one deep hook and chest connected to opponent's upper back
Invisible collar grip deep enough that opponent perceives it as a genuine finishing threat requiring two-handed defense
Seatbelt or underhook control maintained by the non-collar arm to preserve position during transition
Opponent's defensive hands both engaged on the collar grip rather than protecting the neck
Body positioning with hips slightly below opponent's to prevent rolling escape during the switch

execution_steps.description: Secure back control with hooks and seatbelt grip, then gradually walk your over-hook hand into the collar material. Make the grip appear positional rather than threatening to avoid triggering early defensive responses from your opponent. Achieve finger penetration deep enough to apply credible choking pressure.

Incrementally increase collar grip depth by driving fingers deeper into the gi material during moments when your opponent focuses on hook defense or other threats. Apply periodic squeezing pressure to demonstrate genuine finishing potential and force your opponent to perceive the collar as the primary danger requiring immediate attention.

Continue applying intermittent collar pressure until your opponent commits both hands to removing the grip. Monitor their hand positioning carefully and confirm that both hands are fully engaged on your collar wrist and forearm before initiating the transition. Their attention must be focused downward on the collar, not on protecting the chin.

In one fluid motion, release the collar grip and immediately thread your forearm beneath your opponent's chin from the collar side. The blade of your forearm should slide along the side of the neck with your hand reaching toward the opposite shoulder. Their hands remain occupied where the collar grip was, creating a 1-2 second window of unprotected neck access.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds, must be one continuous motion

execution_steps.description: Connect your choking hand to your opposite bicep to establish the figure-four configuration behind the opponent's head. Place your locking hand palm-forward against the back of the skull. This connection must be completed before the opponent can redirect their hands from the abandoned collar grip to the new choking arm threat around their neck.

Squeeze your elbows together while expanding your chest to create compression on both carotid arteries simultaneously. Drive the back of your opponent's head forward with your locking hand while pulling your choking elbow toward your own ribcage. Maintain hook control and chest-to-back connection throughout the finishing sequence to prevent last-moment escape attempts.
execution_steps.timing: 3-5 seconds of progressive pressure in training

execution_steps.description: Maintain steady progressive pressure until your opponent taps or the referee stops the match. The blood choke should produce a tap within 5-8 seconds of full compression when properly applied. Release immediately upon any tap signal, remove hooks, and guide your partner to a side-lying recovery position. Monitor their consciousness and breathing for 30 seconds after release.

common_counters.counter: Opponent strips collar grip early before committing both hands, keeping one hand at the chin
common_counters.your_response: Continue deepening the collar grip with more incremental pressure rather than switching. The goal is to make the collar threat severe enough that one-handed defense is insufficient, forcing them to eventually commit the second hand.

common_counters.counter: Opponent tucks chin aggressively when feeling the collar release, blocking the forearm path
common_counters.your_response: Use the collar drag variation by pulling upward on the collar before releasing to lift the chin. Alternatively, thread the arm across the chin and use the forearm to pry it open, or switch to a short choke by grabbing your own wrist for a tighter circumference.

common_counters.counter: Opponent turns into the attacker and drops hooks during the transition window to escape back control
common_counters.your_response: Maintain chest-to-back connection and use your seatbelt arm to follow their rotation. If they turn far enough, transition to crucifix or follow to mount rather than forcing the RNC. A body triangle before the switch eliminates this escape entirely.

common_counters.counter: Opponent grabs choking wrist with both hands after it threads under the chin, preventing figure-four lock
common_counters.your_response: Use your free hand to peel their grip finger by finger from your wrist, or switch to a palm-to-palm short choke that does not require the figure-four. Their hands on your wrist actually helps the choke if you can connect the lock because they pull the arm tighter against their own neck.

common_errors.error: Releasing the collar grip too slowly or in two stages rather than one fluid motion
common_errors.consequence: The opponent has time to recognize the switch and redirect their hands from collar defense to chin protection, eliminating the transition window entirely
common_errors.correction: Drill the release-and-thread as a single continuous movement. The collar hand should never pause in open space between releasing the collar and contacting the neck. Practice the motion without a partner until it becomes one reflexive action.

common_errors.error: Abandoning seatbelt control with the supporting arm during the collar-to-RNC transition
common_errors.consequence: The opponent escapes back control during the critical moment when the choking arm is in transit, losing both the submission opportunity and dominant position
common_errors.correction: The non-collar arm must maintain active seatbelt or underhook control throughout the entire transition. Never release the supporting arm to assist the threading motion. Your back control depends entirely on this arm during the switch.

common_errors.error: Placing the forearm directly across the trachea instead of the blade against the carotid arteries
common_errors.consequence: Creates a painful but ineffective windpipe crush that causes coughing and tracheal injury rather than a clean blood choke, and gives the opponent more time to escape before losing consciousness
common_errors.correction: Thread the forearm so the bony radius bone aligns against one carotid artery while the bicep compresses the other. The chin should rest in the crook of your elbow, not on top of the forearm. Adjust by rotating your wrist slightly toward the ceiling.

common_errors.error: Attempting the RNC switch when the opponent has only committed one hand to collar defense
common_errors.consequence: The opponent's free hand immediately blocks the choking arm from threading under the chin, wasting the element of surprise and alerting them to the bait-and-switch strategy
common_errors.correction: Wait patiently for confirmed two-handed commitment on the collar before switching. If they defend with one hand, continue deepening the collar threat until the single hand proves insufficient and they are forced to add the second.

common_errors.error: Losing hook control by focusing entirely on the upper body transition during the switch
common_errors.consequence: The opponent hip escapes or slides down during the transition, creating enough space to turn and face the attacker or escape back control completely
common_errors.correction: Actively drive hooks toward the opponent's hips throughout the transition. Consider establishing a body triangle before the switch against opponents known for explosive hip escapes. Lower body control maintains the positional frame while upper body executes the technique.

common_errors.error: Cranking the neck by pulling the head backward rather than squeezing arms together
common_errors.consequence: Creates a neck crank that causes cervical spine injury rather than a blood choke, increases injury risk substantially, and is less effective at producing a submission
common_errors.correction: Focus on squeezing your elbows together and expanding your chest rather than pulling the opponent's head backward. The finishing pressure comes from bilateral arm compression, not from bending the neck. The locking hand pushes the head forward into the choke, not backward.

training_progressions.description: Practice the collar release and arm threading motion without resistance. Partner sits passively while you repeat the transition 20-30 times per side, focusing on making the release-and-thread one continuous fluid motion. Build muscle memory for the hand path from collar to neck.

Partner provides 30-50% resistance and defends the collar with varying levels of hand commitment. Practice identifying the moment both hands engage the collar and executing the switch only when the window is genuinely open. Reset when you mistime the transition.

training_progressions.focus: Complete collar-to-RNC chain under progressive resistance
training_progressions.description: Start from established invisible collar with partner at 50-75% resistance. Execute the full sequence from collar deepening through RNC finish. Partner defends realistically but allows the transition to complete. Focus on maintaining back control throughout and finishing with proper blood choke mechanics.

training_progressions.focus: Full speed application with complete defensive resistance
training_progressions.description: Begin from back control with full resistance. Must establish invisible collar, bait the defense, and execute the RNC transition against an actively resisting partner. Partner uses all available defenses. Track success rate over multiple rounds to identify timing and mechanical improvements needed.

Practice alternating between collar deepening and RNC attempts as a continuous chain. If the RNC fails, return to the collar. If the collar is defended, switch to the RNC. Develop the ability to cycle between both threats fluidly until the finish presents itself against partners who understand both attacks.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Rear Naked Choke from Invisible Collar target?
flashcards.answer: The RNC targets the carotid arteries on both sides of the neck, compressing them to restrict blood flow to the brain. The choking arm's radius bone presses against one carotid while the bicep of the same arm compresses the other. The figure-four lock behind the head creates a sealed compression chamber that eliminates gaps in the circumferential pressure around the neck.

flashcards.question: What indicators confirm your opponent is ready to be caught by the collar-to-RNC transition?
flashcards.answer: Both of the opponent's hands are actively gripping your collar arm, their attention is focused downward toward the collar rather than protecting their chin, and there is a slight forward lean as they strain to strip the grip. When you feel maximum resistance on the collar hand with both their hands fully engaged on your wrist and forearm, the neck is maximally exposed for the transition.
flashcards.answer_line: Both hands gripping the collar arm

flashcards.question: What positional control must be established before attempting the collar-to-RNC transition?
flashcards.answer: You need secure hook control with at least one deep hook, a functioning seatbelt with your non-collar arm that will maintain back control during the switch, and your chest firmly connected to the opponent's upper back. Your hips should be slightly below theirs to prevent rolling escapes. The collar grip must be deep enough that the opponent perceives it as a genuine finishing threat requiring two-handed defense.

flashcards.question: At what point during the transition does the opponent lose the ability to defend effectively?
flashcards.answer: The point of no escape occurs when the choking forearm passes fully under the chin and your hand contacts the opposite bicep to form the figure-four lock. Once this connection is established, even loosely, the opponent cannot remove the arm without first breaking the lock. The critical window is the 1-2 seconds between collar release and bicep connection. If you achieve this before they redirect their hands, the finish is virtually guaranteed.

flashcards.question: Your opponent manages to get one hand inside the choke before the figure-four locks—what grip adjustment maintains finishing pressure?
flashcards.answer: Do not try to overpower their defending hand. Switch to a short choke by gripping your own wrist instead of the bicep, which narrows the choke circumference and can trap their defending hand against their own neck. Alternatively, use your free hand to peel their fingers from your wrist one at a time. Their hand inside the choke actually increases pressure on one carotid if you can complete the lock around it.

flashcards.question: What are the critical finishing errors that reduce effectiveness and increase injury risk?
flashcards.answer: The most dangerous error is placing the forearm directly across the trachea, creating a windpipe crush instead of a blood choke. Other common errors include cranking the neck backward by pulling the head rather than squeezing elbows together, failing to use the locking hand to push the head forward into the choke, and applying explosive jerking force rather than progressive steady compression. Each error reduces submission effectiveness while increasing injury risk substantially.

flashcards.question: What safety precautions are essential when training the RNC from Invisible Collar?
flashcards.answer: Apply pressure progressively over 3-5 seconds minimum and never snap or jerk the choke. Ensure the forearm blade sits against the carotid arteries, not the trachea. Release immediately upon any tap signal including verbal, physical hand tap, foot tap, or going limp. After release, monitor your partner for 30 seconds minimum and keep them lying down if they lost consciousness. Never hold past the tap under any circumstances regardless of training context.

flashcards.question: What is the proper release protocol if your training partner loses consciousness during this choke?
flashcards.answer: Immediately release all choking pressure and remove your hooks and body control. Guide your partner gently to a side-lying recovery position. Do not allow them to sit or stand until they are fully conscious and oriented. Monitor their breathing and responsiveness. If they do not regain consciousness within 20 seconds, call for medical assistance immediately. Keep them lying flat for at least 2-3 minutes after regaining consciousness before allowing them to resume activity.

flashcards.question: How do you create the collar-to-RNC dilemma effectively against an experienced opponent who knows the switch?
flashcards.answer: Against experienced opponents, the collar threat must be genuinely dangerous before the RNC switch becomes viable. Incrementally deepen the collar grip over 15-30 seconds with periodic squeezing to demonstrate real finishing intent. Only attempt the switch when you feel the opponent escalate to two-handed defense. If they only commit one hand, continue deepening. Chain multiple collar-RNC-collar cycles to deteriorate their defensive timing over time rather than relying on a single transition attempt.

trap: Switch the moment one hand grips

flashcards.question: During competition, what adjustments maximize submission probability with this technique?
flashcards.answer: In competition, time the transition for peak defensive commitment. Use incremental collar pressure to build urgency, then switch explosively rather than gradually. Once the RNC connects, immediately lock the figure-four and begin squeezing rather than adjusting for perfect position. Combine with a body triangle to eliminate hip escape during the finish. The combination of surprise from the switch and immediate finishing pressure catches elite defenders who expect time to address each threat sequentially.

defender.name: from Invisible Collar Defender
defender.description: Defend the Rear Naked Choke from Invisible Collar. Recognize the collar-to-RNC switch, protect your neck, and escape back control with proven methods.
defender.overview: Defending the Rear Naked Choke from Invisible Collar demands awareness that the collar grip may be bait for the RNC rather than a direct choke threat. The primary challenge is managing the collar defense without overcommitting both hands, which creates the exact opening the attacker seeks for the choking arm. Effective defense requires keeping one hand available for neck protection at all times, even while addressing the collar grip, and recognizing the transition moment when the attacker releases the collar so you can redirect defensive resources immediately to the chin and neck. The defender who understands this dilemma structure can break the cycle by refusing to give the attacker the two-handed commitment window they need.
key_principles: Never commit both hands to collar removal simultaneously—always keep one hand available for chin and neck protection
Recognize the collar grip as potential RNC bait rather than treating it exclusively as a direct choking threat
Maintain an aggressive chin tuck throughout all defensive actions to limit the threading angle for the choking arm
Monitor the attacker's collar hand for the release movement that signals the RNC transition is beginning
Coordinate hand fighting with hip escape to address both grip control and positional escape simultaneously
Time explosive escape attempts for the transition moment when the attacker's choking arm is between collar and neck
Prioritize escaping back control entirely over simply defending individual submission attempts
recognition_cues: Attacker's collar grip hand appears to be controlling rather than actively finishing, with intermittent pressure that invites your defensive hand commitment
Attacker maintains patient positioning and does not rush the collar finish despite having depth, suggesting they are waiting for your defensive reaction
You feel the attacker's collar hand suddenly release tension or let go of the gi material entirely, signaling the transition to RNC threading
Attacker watches your hand positioning rather than focusing on their own grip depth, indicating they are reading your defense to time the switch

defensive_options.action: One-handed collar defense with chin protection
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you recognize the invisible collar grip being established, before it becomes deep enough to force two-handed removal
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the attacker from establishing the dilemma by keeping one hand permanently stationed at your chin while the other addresses the collar
defensive_options.risk: One-handed collar defense is slower and may not prevent deep grip establishment, but preserves neck protection

defensive_options.action: Immediate chin tuck and hip escape upon collar release
defensive_options.when_to_use: The instant you feel the collar grip release, which signals the RNC transition is beginning
defensive_options.if_successful: Your chin blocks the choking arm from threading beneath while your hip escape creates distance that may allow you to turn and recover guard
defensive_options.risk: Requires precise timing—too slow and the arm threads before your chin drops, too early and you may be reacting to a false release

defensive_options.action: Turn toward the choking arm side and fight to closed guard
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the RNC arm has partially threaded but the figure-four lock is not yet secured, and you still have hook clearance to rotate
defensive_options.if_successful: Escaping back control entirely by turning into the attacker, clearing hooks, and establishing closed guard from the front
defensive_options.risk: Turning into a partially locked RNC can tighten it if you mistime the rotation—only attempt when the lock is not connected

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one wrist control on the choking arm
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the RNC arm has threaded under the chin but the figure-four is not yet locked, as an emergency defensive measure
defensive_options.if_successful: Stripping the choking arm away from the neck and returning to a position where the attacker must re-establish the submission setup
defensive_options.risk: Committing both hands to the wrist leaves you vulnerable to the attacker switching back to the collar or transitioning to an armbar

escape_paths: Hip escape toward the non-collar side while maintaining chin tuck to create space for turning into half guard or closed guard
Turn toward the choking arm side and clear hooks to recover to closed guard before the figure-four lock connects
Stand up escape by removing hooks with hand fighting while keeping chin tucked and one hand protecting the neck

favorable_outcomes.how: Time your turn and hook removal for the transition moment when the attacker releases the collar. Use the 1-2 second window while their choking arm is in transit to rotate, clear hooks, and establish closed guard facing the attacker.

common_errors.error: Committing both hands to collar grip removal, leaving the neck completely unprotected
common_errors.consequence: Creates the exact opening the attacker needs to release the collar and thread the choking arm under an undefended chin with no resistance
common_errors.correction: Always keep one hand stationed at your chin or neck even while addressing the collar grip. Accept slower collar defense in exchange for permanent neck protection. Use hip movement and body positioning to supplement the single-handed collar defense.

common_errors.error: Failing to recognize the collar grip as RNC bait until the transition is already happening
common_errors.consequence: The choking arm threads under the chin before defensive hands can redirect from the abandoned collar position to the neck, leaving no time to prevent the figure-four lock
common_errors.correction: Treat every invisible collar grip as a potential RNC setup. Develop the habit of maintaining chin protection regardless of what the collar hand is doing. Practice recognition drills where the attacker randomly switches between collar finish and RNC to build identification speed.

common_errors.error: Extending the chin upward or away from the chest while struggling to remove the collar grip
common_errors.consequence: Creates additional space beneath the chin for the choking arm to thread and increases the angle of attack for both the collar finish and the RNC transition
common_errors.correction: Maintain an aggressive chin tuck pressed hard against your chest throughout all defensive movements. The chin tuck is your primary physical barrier against the choking arm regardless of which submission the attacker pursues.

common_errors.error: Panicking and using random explosive movements without addressing the specific threat
common_errors.consequence: Burns energy rapidly while potentially creating better openings for the attacker by disrupting your own defensive structure and hook control
common_errors.correction: Follow a systematic defensive sequence: protect chin first, then address the specific grip threat with one hand, then work hip escape and hook removal with coordinated movement. Save explosive efforts for identified escape windows during the attacker's grip transitions.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the invisible collar grip is being used as bait for an RNC rather than a direct finishing threat?
flashcards.answer: The attacker applies intermittent collar pressure rather than progressive finishing force, maintains patient positioning despite having grip depth, and appears to be monitoring your hand positioning rather than focusing on deepening their own grip. If the collar pressure feels like it is inviting your defensive reaction rather than building toward a finish, they are likely setting up the RNC switch.

flashcards.question: What is the safest approach to tapping when caught in the RNC from Invisible Collar?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately when you feel blood choke pressure building and your defense is failing. Use a clear physical tap on the attacker's arm, your own body, or the mat, supplemented by a verbal tap saying the word aloud. If your arms are trapped, tap with your feet on the mat. The blood choke can cause unconsciousness within 5-8 seconds of full compression, so there is no advantage to waiting when the lock is secured.

flashcards.question: What is the critical defensive mistake that creates the RNC opening from invisible collar?
flashcards.answer: The critical mistake is committing both hands to removing the collar grip simultaneously. This is exactly what the attacker needs because it leaves the chin and neck completely unprotected for the 1-2 seconds required to release the collar and thread the choking arm. Instead, always keep one hand available for chin and neck protection even if it means slower collar defense with the remaining hand.

trap: Keep one hand on the neck

flashcards.question: When is the optimal moment to attempt an escape during the collar-to-RNC transition?
flashcards.answer: The optimal escape window is during the 1-2 seconds when the attacker's choking arm is in transit between the collar and the neck. At this moment, their attacking arm has no grip on anything and their control is at its weakest point. If you time a hip escape and turn for this exact moment, you can exploit the gap in their control before the RNC arm threads under your chin.
flashcards.answer_line: Arm in transit, no grip yet

flashcards.question: How should you manage your energy when defending repeated collar-to-RNC cycling from an attacker?
flashcards.answer: Maintain a sustainable defensive posture with chin tucked and one hand protecting the neck at all times rather than using explosive bursts for each individual threat. The attacker wants to fatigue your defense through repeated cycling, so efficient defensive positioning is more important than powerful individual responses. Save your explosive energy for a committed escape attempt when you identify a genuine opening during their grip transition moment.

training_progressions.description: Partner establishes invisible collar and randomly either finishes the collar choke or switches to RNC. Defender must identify which attack is coming within 2 seconds and respond with the appropriate defense. Track recognition accuracy over 20 repetitions to build pattern identification.

training_progressions.focus: Maintaining neck protection while addressing collar grip
training_progressions.description: Practice defending the invisible collar using only one hand on the grip while the other stays permanently at the chin. Partner provides 40-60% resistance and periodically attempts the RNC switch. Builds the habit of never committing both hands to the collar and maintaining constant neck defense.

training_progressions.focus: Exploiting the transition window for escape
training_progressions.description: Partner executes the collar-to-RNC switch at realistic speed. Defender practices timing the hip escape and turn for the exact moment the collar releases. Start at slow speed and increase progressively as timing improves. The goal is consistent escape during the 1-2 second transition window.

training_progressions.focus: Complete defensive application against unrestricted back attacks
training_progressions.description: Start with attacker in invisible collar position. Defender must survive and escape within 2 minutes against full resistance. Attacker can use any back attack including collar finish, RNC switch, armbar, or crucifix. Builds defensive composure and decision-making under realistic pressure.

clips.title: Preventing the Hand Crossing to the Other Side
Turtle No-Grips Escape Rolling to Guard
